CS4423 overview

CS4423 Topic Guide

Prufer Codes and Trees

Encode a labelled tree by repeatedly removing its smallest leaf.

Purpose and relevance

Prufer codes establish a one-to-one correspondence between labelled trees on n vertices and sequences of length n−2. They are a recurring specialist calculation topic.Exam use: Word length, smallest-leaf rule, every emitted edge and the degree-frequency identity all verify the result.

What a question really asks — answer plan

For encoding, state the tie rule, remove the smallest labelled leaf, record its neighbour and repeat n−2 times. For decoding, repeatedly join the first code element to the smallest label absent from the remaining code.Question interpretation: For encode, repeatedly remove the smallest labelled leaf; for decode, choose the smallest label absent from the remaining code; for count, apply Cayley's formula only to labelled trees.

Prerequisites, vocabulary and formulas

  • A tree on n vertices has n−1 edges.
  • Prufer sequence length = n−2.
  • deg(v)=1 + occurrences of v in the Prufer code.
  • Number of labelled trees on n vertices is nⁿ⁻² (Cayley’s formula).
  • Rapid recall: A tree on n labelled vertices has a Prufer word of length n-2; label v appears deg(v)-1 times; there are n^{n-2} labelled trees.

Step-by-step method

  1. Encoding: find smallest leaf; write its neighbour; delete leaf.
  2. Continue until two vertices remain.
  3. Decoding: choose smallest label absent from current code.
  4. Join it to first entry, delete both; finally join the last two labels.
  5. Exam workflow: Keep a live degree table from code frequencies, update it after each emitted edge, and finish by joining the last two degree-one vertices.

Worked starter question and model answer

Question: Decode [2,2] on labels {1,2,3,4}.

Model answer: Smallest absent is 1: add 1-2. Remaining [2], smallest absent is 3: add 3-2. Join remaining 2-4. Degrees are 1,3,1,1, agreeing with occurrences plus one.

Medium/hard paper-style synthesis

Decode code (4,4,2) on {1,2,3,4,5}. Initial degrees from frequencies are d=(1,2,1,3,1). Smallest leaf 1 joins 4; now 3 joins 4; 4 becomes a leaf and joins 2; finally leaves 2 and 5 join. Edges are {14,34,24,25}. Degrees (1,2,1,3,1) match occurrence counts plus one.

Graduated practice

Prompt 1

What is code length for a 7-vertex tree? Check: 5.

Exam bridge

Encode a labelled tree, reconstruct it, and infer its degree sequence from the code. Check: show every leaf choice, use the smallest-label rule, end with final edge, then use occurrences+1.

Hard paper-style synthesis

Paper-style synthesis: encode the tree with edges {12,13,34,35,56}. Check remove leaves 2, then 1, then 4, then 3, recording neighbours (1,3,3,5); length 4=n-2.

Practice question - decode and audit a Prüfer code [8 marks]

Inspired by: CS4423 2024/25 Q5(b-c). Scenario. Decode the Prüfer code (4,4,2) on labels {1,2,3,4,5}, and give the degree sequence. [8 marks]

Demand diagnosis and fastest route: show each smallest-leaf choice; degree can be checked from occurrence counts plus one.

Worked answer: Initially the labels absent from the code are leaves 1,3,5. Join smallest leaf 1 to first code entry 4, remove 1 and that entry. Leaves are now 3,5; join 3 to 4. Now 4 no longer occurs and becomes a leaf, so join 4 to 2. The two labels left are 2 and 5, giving final edge 2-5. Thus E={14,34,24,25}. Occurrences in the code are (0,1,0,2,0), so degrees are (1,2,1,3,1), agreeing with the constructed tree.

Topic-specific trap: choose the smallest currently available leaf, not the smallest label that has ever been absent.

Common mistakes

  • Recording the leaf rather than its neighbour.
  • Using arbitrary rather than stated smallest-leaf tie-breaking.
  • Forgetting the final edge in decoding.
  • Recovery rule: During decoding, choose the smallest label absent from the current remaining suffix, not absent from the original code.

Final checklist

  • Is length n−2?
  • Did I show deletions?
  • Did I verify degrees?
  • Final 60-second audit: Word length, smallest-leaf rule, every emitted edge and the degree-frequency identity all verify the result.

Past-paper note

Prufer encoding, decoding and degree questions recur in local 2017/18–2024/25 papers but are less central than BFS/centrality/random graphs.
